newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu, Clinton to chart peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu, Clinton to chart peace moves.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, having closed his first deal with the Palestinians, flies to Washington on Wednesday to chart future Middle East peace moves with Israel's closest ally.

The Israeli leader, who took office eight months ago, will meet U.S. President Bill Clinton at the White House on Thursday for the first time since handing over most of the volatile West Bank town of Hebron to PLO rule in January.

"We're after Hebron and we're looking to see where the strategy for the Middle East peace process turns. Where will the emphasis be placed?" Dore Gold, Netanyahu's foreign policy adviser, told Reuters.

Peace with Palestinians and Syria will top the Israeli agenda. Officials said Netanyahu, elected on a promise to meet security needs, will outline the "red lines" -- or limits -- to Israeli flexibility with the Palestinians.

Officials expect that Clinton, sworn in for a second term last month, will also promise to help search for a "bridging formula" for reviving peace talks with Syria broken off by Israel nearly a year ago.

Netanyahu will meet new Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and new Defence Secretary William Cohen during a two-day stay in Washington. He will spend Saturday, the Jewish sabbath, in New York before flying home.
He will also meet leaders of Congress, which gave him a standing ovation on his first post-election visit last year and gives Israel $3 billion a year in aid, the highest sum given any country.

The meeting with Clinton is the first since the right-wing Netanyahu carried out any part of the deals with the PLO he reluctantly inherited from Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres, the Labour party leader he ousted in May.
Clinton and Netanyahu, joined by the Palestinians' Yasser Arafat, last met in October after violence over Netanyahu's opening of a new entrance to a Jerusalem tourist tunnel near a Moslem shrine.

Since then Netanyahu has given 80 percent of Hebron's Palestinians self-rule, agreed to free Palestinian prisoners -- 31 of them women on Tuesday -- and set three more deadlines for pulling troops out of West Bank rural areas starting on March 7.

So far Netanyahu says his Likud party is only carrying out the "interim agreement" signed by the governments of Peres and Yitzhak Rabin, assassinated in 1995 by a Jew opposed to his unprecedented land-for-peace deals with Palestinians.

When he meets Clinton for three hours on Thursday, Netanyahu will lay out a blueprint for talks on "final-status" issues such as Jewish settlers, the return of refugees, borders, the fate of Jerusalem and the question of Palestinian statehood.

"We are bound by the agreement known as the interim agreement. The real leeway is in the 'final status' and we are going to present our case in terms of what we need to keep Israel secure," said a senior Israeli official.

Jewish settlements in occupied Arab lands are one U.S.-Israeli bone of contention that could come up on Thursday. Clinton has called them an obstacle to peace. Netanyahu's government backs the more than 130,000 settlers.
Arafat is due to pay a White House visit in early March.

Talks with Syria, seen as the cornerstone to an overall Middle East peace, have long been stuck over the fate of the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Damascus wants the heights back; Israel says no.
Netanyahu will demand Syria stop guerrillas from Hizbollah, the "Party of God", from attacking Israeli soldiers in south Lebanon.

The Israeli leader shortened his planned U.S. trip by about two days following the death of 73 Lebanon-bound soldiers in the collision of two helicopters last week, the worst military air disaster in the country's 49-year history.
